subject: history

moments.title: Truman Doctrine
moments.body: 12 March 1947: Truman addresses Congress to pledge aid to Greece and Turkey to resist communist insurgency. The framing — 'free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation' — extends US commitment beyond the wartime alliance to general containment of Soviet expansion.

quote.text: It must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.

moments.takeaway: George Kennan's 'Long Telegram' (February 1946) and 'X-Article' (July 1947) provided the intellectual basis for containment.

moments.title: Marshall Plan announced
moments.body: 5 June 1947: Secretary of State Marshall announces a European Recovery Programme at Harvard. From 1948-1952, around $13 billion (over $150 billion in 2020 dollars) flows to 16 Western European countries. The USSR and Eastern bloc refuse participation.
moments.takeaway: The Plan paired economic generosity with strategic intent — preventing communist victory in war-shattered Western Europe.

moments.title: Berlin Blockade and Airlift
moments.body: June 1948: Stalin blockades West Berlin's land routes after the Western introduction of the Deutsche Mark. The Berlin Airlift — over 200,000 flights, 1.5 million tonnes of supplies — keeps West Berlin fed for 11 months. Stalin lifts the blockade in May 1949.
moments.takeaway: NATO is founded April 1949. The Federal Republic of Germany follows in May, the GDR in October. Europe is now formally divided.

now.title: Cold War aftermath
now.body: The framework of containment shaped US foreign policy until 1991 — and arguably beyond. NATO's expansion east since 1999, current tensions with Russia over Ukraine (2014, 2022) and the broader 'great power competition' framing draw on Cold War institutional inheritance. The Marshall Plan remains a reference point for international aid packages.
now.open_questions: Was the Cold War inevitable from 1945? John Lewis Gaddis's 'We Now Know' (1997) emphasises Stalin's expansion as the driver; revisionists (Melvyn Leffler) emphasise US responses; post-revisionists balance both.

reflection: The Cold War was framed by economic and diplomatic moves before it was a nuclear standoff. Marshall Aid, the Truman Doctrine and the Berlin Airlift built the political-economic shape of the West for decades.
